CHAPTER 18 - RANDOM EXPERIMENTS AND EVENTS

Introduction

When we toss a coin we cannot say in advance whether a head or a tail will turn up; when we roll a die we cannot predict which of the six faces will show. Yet we know perfectly well the complete list of things that COULD happen. Experiments of this kind - whose individual result cannot be foretold but whose set of possible results is known - are called RANDOM experiments, and they are the foundation of the theory of probability. This chapter introduces the basic language of that theory: the random experiment, the trial, the outcome, the sample space, and the events that are built as subsets of the sample space. We then study the different TYPES of events and the ALGEBRA of events (union, intersection, complement and difference), and finally the important ideas of mutually exclusive, exhaustive and equally likely events. Mastering this vocabulary is essential before probabilities can be calculated in later chapters.

18.1 RANDOM EXPERIMENTS, TRIALS AND OUTCOMES

An EXPERIMENT is an operation that produces some well-defined results. Experiments are of two kinds. A DETERMINISTIC experiment is one whose result is certain and can be predicted exactly - for example, mixing hydrogen and oxygen under fixed conditions always gives water, or heating water to 100 degrees Celsius at normal pressure always makes it boil. A RANDOM (or probabilistic) experiment is one that satisfies three conditions:
 (i) it can be repeated any number of times under identical conditions;
 (ii) all its possible results (outcomes) are known in advance; and
 (iii) the actual result on any particular performance cannot be predicted with certainty.
Tossing a coin, throwing a die, drawing a card from a well-shuffled pack, and drawing a ball from a bag of coloured balls are all random experiments.

A TRIAL is a single performance of a random experiment. Tossing a coin once is one trial; throwing a die once is one trial. The result of a trial is called an OUTCOME (or sample point). For example, in the toss of a coin the outcomes are 'head' (H) and 'tail' (T); in the throw of a die the outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Each outcome is one of the possible elementary results of the experiment.

18.2 SAMPLE SPACE

The SAMPLE SPACE of a random experiment is the SET of ALL possible outcomes. It is usually denoted by S (some books use the Greek letter). Each element of the sample space is a sample point, and the number of sample points is written n(S). Listing the sample space is the very first step in analysing any random experiment.

Some standard sample spaces:
 - Tossing one coin: S = {H, T}, n(S) = 2.
 - Tossing two coins (or one coin twice): S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, n(S) = 4.
 - Tossing three coins: S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT}, n(S) = 8. In general, tossing n coins gives 2^n outcomes.
 - Throwing one die: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, n(S) = 6.
 - Throwing two dice: each outcome is an ordered pair (a, b) with a the first die and b the second, so S = {(1,1), (1,2), ..., (6,6)}, n(S) = 36.
 - Drawing a card from a standard pack: n(S) = 52 (four suits - spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs - each with 13 cards).
 - Drawing a ball from a bag containing balls of different colours: the sample space is the list of the individual balls.
A sample space may be FINITE (a countable, limited list, like the ones above) or INFINITE (for example, counting the number of tosses of a coin until the first head appears). In this chapter we work mainly with finite sample spaces.

18.3 EVENTS

An EVENT is any SUBSET of the sample space S. In words, an event is a collection of outcomes to which we can attach a description. When we perform the experiment and the outcome that occurs belongs to the event, we say the event has OCCURRED; otherwise the event has NOT occurred. For example, in throwing a die let A be the event 'an even number appears'. Then A = {2, 4, 6}. If the die shows 4, the outcome 4 is in A, so A has occurred; if the die shows 3, then 3 is not in A, so A has not occurred.

Because an event is a set, the number of outcomes favourable to an event A is written n(A). Since A is a subset of S, we always have 0 <= n(A) <= n(S).

18.4 TYPES OF EVENTS

SIMPLE (or ELEMENTARY) EVENT: an event that contains EXACTLY ONE outcome (one sample point). In the throw of a die, 'getting a 5', i.e. {5}, is a simple event. A sample space with n(S) points has exactly n(S) simple events.

COMPOUND (or COMPOSITE) EVENT: an event that contains MORE THAN ONE outcome. 'Getting an even number' = {2, 4, 6} in the throw of a die is a compound event because it is made up of several sample points.

SURE (or CERTAIN) EVENT: the event that is CERTAIN to happen. It contains ALL the outcomes, so it is the whole sample space S itself. In the throw of a die, 'getting a number less than 7' = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S is a sure event - it must occur on every trial.

IMPOSSIBLE EVENT: an event that can NEVER happen. It contains no outcome at all, so it is the EMPTY set (written { } or the null set). In the throw of a die, 'getting a 7' is impossible; the corresponding subset has no sample points.

COMPLEMENTARY EVENT: the complement of an event A, written A' (also A-bar or 'not A'), is the set of all outcomes in the sample space that are NOT in A. If A = {2, 4, 6} (even number on a die), then A' = {1, 3, 5} (odd number). The event A' occurs exactly when A does not occur. Note that A and A' together contain every outcome, and they share none, so n(A) + n(A') = n(S).

18.5 ALGEBRA OF EVENTS

Since events are sets, we can combine them using the operations of set theory. Let A and B be two events of the same sample space S.

UNION (A union B), written A U B, is the event 'A OR B' - the set of outcomes that belong to A, or to B, or to both. It occurs when AT LEAST ONE of A and B occurs. Example (die): if A = {2, 4, 6} (even) and B = {3, 6} (multiples of 3), then A union B = {2, 3, 4, 6}.

INTERSECTION (A intersect B), written A n B, is the event 'A AND B' - the set of outcomes common to both A and B. It occurs when BOTH A and B occur together. For the same A and B, A intersect B = {6} (the outcome that is both even and a multiple of 3).

COMPLEMENT of A, written A', is 'NOT A' - the outcomes of S not in A, as defined above.

DIFFERENCE, written A - B (read 'A but not B'), is the set of outcomes that are in A but NOT in B. For the example, A - B = {2, 4} (even numbers that are not multiples of 3), and B - A = {3} (multiples of 3 that are not even). Note A - B = A intersect B'.

Some useful facts that follow from set theory:
 - A union A' = S and A intersect A' = { } (the empty set).
 - (A')' = A.
 - De Morgan's laws: (A union B)' = A' intersect B' and (A intersect B)' = A' union B'.
 - A union B = B union A and A intersect B = B intersect A (commutative).
The event 'A occurs but B does not' is A intersect B'; the event 'neither A nor B' is A' intersect B' = (A union B)'; the event 'exactly one of A and B' is (A intersect B') union (A' intersect B).

18.6 MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (DISJOINT) EVENTS

Two events A and B are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (or DISJOINT, or incompatible) if they CANNOT happen together - that is, they have no outcome in common. In set language,
   A intersect B = { } (the empty set).
For example, in the throw of a die, A = 'even number' = {2, 4, 6} and C = 'odd number' = {1, 3, 5} are mutually exclusive, because no number is both even and odd; A intersect C = { }. The two simple events {1} and {2} are always mutually exclusive. Any event A and its complement A' are mutually exclusive, since A intersect A' = { }. When several events are mutually exclusive in pairs, at most one of them can occur on a single trial.

18.7 EXHAUSTIVE EVENTS

A set of events is EXHAUSTIVE if TOGETHER they include EVERY possible outcome of the experiment - that is, their union is the whole sample space S. For events A1, A2, ..., Ak,
   A1 union A2 union ... union Ak = S.
For example, in the throw of a die, the events A = {1, 2}, B = {3, 4} and C = {5, 6} are exhaustive because A union B union C = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S. An event A and its complement A' are always exhaustive (A union A' = S) as well as mutually exclusive.

MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE AND EXHAUSTIVE SYSTEM: a collection of events that is BOTH mutually exclusive (no two share an outcome) AND exhaustive (their union is S) is called a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system, or a PARTITION of the sample space. Every outcome of S then belongs to EXACTLY ONE of the events. The pair A and A' is the simplest such system. In the die example, {1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6} form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system, and so do the six simple events {1}, {2}, {3}, {4}, {5}, {6}.

18.8 EQUALLY LIKELY EVENTS

Outcomes (or events) are said to be EQUALLY LIKELY if, considering the nature of the experiment, there is no reason to expect any one of them in preference to another - each has the SAME chance of occurring. When a coin is UNBIASED (fair), head and tail are equally likely; when a die is FAIR, the six faces are equally likely; the 52 cards of a well-shuffled pack are equally likely to be drawn. Equally likely outcomes are the basis of the classical definition of probability, in which the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes. If the coin or die is BIASED (loaded), the outcomes are NOT equally likely. The idea of equally likely outcomes is a modelling assumption about symmetry, not something that can be proved by logic alone.

18.9 OCCURRENCE AND NON-OCCURRENCE OF EVENTS - A SUMMARY OF THE LANGUAGE

Let a random experiment be performed and let its outcome be the sample point w. For an event A:
 - 'A occurs' means w belongs to A.
 - 'A does not occur' means w belongs to A' (the complement).
 - 'A or B occurs' means w belongs to A union B.
 - 'A and B occur' means w belongs to A intersect B.
 - 'A occurs but B does not' means w belongs to A intersect B'.
Thus every ordinary sentence about the experiment can be translated into a statement about sets - this is exactly what makes the set-theory language so powerful for probability. Illustrations from dice, coins and cards recur throughout: for two dice, 'the sum is 7' is the event {(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)}; for a pack of cards, 'a king' is a 4-element event and 'a spade' is a 13-element event, and 'a king AND a spade' is the single card, the king of spades.

SUMMARY

- A RANDOM experiment can be repeated under identical conditions, has all outcomes known in advance, but its particular result cannot be predicted. A single performance is a TRIAL and its result is an OUTCOME.
- The SAMPLE SPACE S is the set of all outcomes; n(S) is the number of sample points. Standard cases: one coin {H,T}; two coins {HH,HT,TH,TT}; a die {1,...,6}; two dice 36 pairs; a pack 52 cards.
- An EVENT is a subset of S; it OCCURS when the observed outcome lies in it. n(A) is the number of favourable outcomes, 0 <= n(A) <= n(S).
- Types of events: SIMPLE (one outcome); COMPOUND (more than one); SURE/CERTAIN (= S); IMPOSSIBLE (the empty set); COMPLEMENTARY A' (not A), with n(A) + n(A') = n(S).
- ALGEBRA of events: union A U B (A or B, at least one); intersection A n B (A and B, both); complement A' (not A); difference A - B = A intersect B' (A but not B). A union A' = S, A intersect A' = { }, and De Morgan's laws hold.
- MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (disjoint) events cannot occur together: A intersect B = { }. EXHAUSTIVE events together cover S: their union = S. A collection that is both is a mutually exclusive and exhaustive SYSTEM (partition); A and A' are the simplest example.
- EQUALLY LIKELY outcomes have the same chance (a fair coin, a fair die, a shuffled pack); this symmetry assumption underlies the classical definition of probability.

topics.name: Random Experiments and Trials
topics.description: The meaning of a random (probabilistic) experiment as one that is repeatable under identical conditions with all outcomes known but the particular result unpredictable; the distinction from a deterministic experiment; the ideas of a trial (one performance) and an outcome (sample point).

topics.name: Sample Space
topics.description: The sample space S as the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment and n(S) as the number of sample points; writing sample spaces for coins, dice and cards; finite and infinite sample spaces.

topics.name: Events and their Types
topics.description: An event as a subset of the sample space and its occurrence/non-occurrence; simple (elementary) and compound events; sure (certain) and impossible events; the complementary event A' with n(A) + n(A') = n(S).

topics.name: Algebra of Events (Union, Intersection, Complement)
topics.description: Combining events using set operations: union A U B (A or B), intersection A n B (A and B), complement A' (not A) and difference A - B = A intersect B'; De Morgan's laws and the identities A U A' = S, A n A' = empty.

topics.name: Mutually Exclusive and Exhaustive Events
topics.description: Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events that cannot occur together (A intersect B = empty); exhaustive events whose union is the whole sample space; a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system (partition) of S, of which A and A' are the simplest example.

topics.name: Equally Likely Events and Event Systems
topics.description: Equally likely outcomes as those with the same chance of occurring for a fair coin, fair die or well-shuffled pack; biased versus unbiased experiments; the role of equally likely outcomes and event systems in the classical description of probability.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain what a random experiment is, distinguish it from a deterministic experiment, and define the terms trial and outcome with suitable examples.
Define the sample space of a random experiment, identify sample points, and state n(S) for standard experiments involving coins, dice and cards.
Write down (list) the sample space and compute n(S) for experiments such as tossing several coins, throwing one or two dice, and drawing cards or balls.
Define an event as a subset of the sample space and classify events as simple, compound, sure, impossible or complementary, using n(A) + n(A') = n(S).
Form and interpret the union, intersection, complement and difference of events, translate verbal statements into set language, and apply De Morgan's laws.
Define mutually exclusive (disjoint) and exhaustive events and recognise them in experiments with dice, coins and cards.
Analyse collections of events to decide whether they form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system (partition) of the sample space.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Equally Likely Events and Event Systems
learning_outcomes.description: Explain the meaning of equally likely outcomes, distinguish biased from unbiased experiments, and relate equally likely outcomes to the classical description of probability.

sections.heading: Random experiments, trials and outcomes
bullets: A random experiment can be repeated under identical conditions, has all outcomes known in advance, but its particular result cannot be predicted.
A deterministic experiment, by contrast, always gives the same predictable result.
A trial is one performance of the experiment; the result of a trial is an outcome (sample point).
Tossing a coin, throwing a die, and drawing a card are standard random experiments.

sections.heading: Sample space
bullets: The sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes; n(S) is the number of sample points.
One coin: S = {H, T}; two coins: {HH, HT, TH, TT}; n coins give 2^n outcomes.
One die: S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}; two dice give 36 ordered pairs; a pack has 52 cards.
A sample space may be finite or infinite; here we mostly use finite ones.

sections.heading: Events and their types
bullets: An event is a subset of S and occurs when the observed outcome lies in it.
Simple event = one outcome; compound event = more than one outcome.
Sure (certain) event = S; impossible event = the empty set.
The complement A' is 'not A', with n(A) + n(A') = n(S).

sections.heading: Algebra of events
bullets: Union A U B is 'A or B' (at least one occurs); intersection A n B is 'A and B' (both occur).
Complement A' is 'not A'; difference A - B = A intersect B' is 'A but not B'.
A U A' = S and A n A' = empty; also (A')' = A.
De Morgan's laws: (A U B)' = A' n B' and (A n B)' = A' U B'.

sections.heading: Mutually exclusive, exhaustive and equally likely events
bullets: Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events cannot occur together: A intersect B = empty.
Exhaustive events together cover the whole sample space: their union = S.
A mutually exclusive AND exhaustive system partitions S; A and A' are the simplest example.
Equally likely outcomes have the same chance (fair coin, fair die, shuffled pack) and underlie classical probability.

key_takeaways: A random experiment is repeatable with known outcomes but an unpredictable particular result; one performance is a trial, its result an outcome.
The sample space S lists all outcomes; standard cases are {H,T}, {HH,HT,TH,TT}, a die {1..6}, two dice (36), a pack (52).
An event is a subset of S and occurs when the outcome belongs to it; n(A) counts favourable outcomes.
Events are simple, compound, sure (= S), impossible (empty) or complementary (A', with n(A)+n(A')=n(S)).
The algebra of events uses union (or), intersection (and), complement (not) and difference (A but not B), with De Morgan's laws.
Mutually exclusive events cannot co-occur (A n B = empty); exhaustive events cover S; both together form a partition.
Equally likely outcomes (fair coin, fair die, shuffled pack) provide the symmetry behind the classical definition of probability.

glossary.definition: An experiment that is repeatable under identical conditions with all outcomes known, but whose particular result cannot be predicted.
An experiment whose result is certain and can be predicted exactly under given conditions.
A single performance of a random experiment, such as one toss of a coin.
The result of a single trial; also called a sample point.
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment; n(S) is the number of sample points.
Any subset of the sample space; it occurs when the observed outcome belongs to it.
An event containing exactly one outcome (one sample point).
An event containing more than one outcome.
The event equal to the whole sample space S; it is certain to occur.
The event equal to the empty set; it can never occur.
The set of outcomes not in A, i.e. 'not A'; n(A) + n(A') = n(S).
The event 'A or B' - outcomes in A, in B, or in both; occurs when at least one occurs.
The event 'A and B' - outcomes common to both A and B; occurs when both occur.
Events with no common outcome (A intersect B = empty); they cannot occur together.
Events whose union is the whole sample space, so at least one of them must occur.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Random Experiments and Events (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. For each experiment, write the sample space clearly before finding events. Use set notation (union, intersection, complement) where required and show your reasoning.

questions.question: Define a random experiment and state the three conditions it must satisfy. Give one example.
questions.answer:
A random experiment is an experiment whose particular result cannot be predicted in advance, even though the set of all possible results is known. It must satisfy three conditions:
(i) it can be repeated any number of times under identical conditions;
(ii) all its possible outcomes are known in advance; and
(iii) the actual outcome on any particular trial cannot be predicted with certainty.
Example: tossing a fair coin - we know the outcomes are head and tail, but we cannot say which will appear on a given toss.
questions.explanation: Definition + three conditions + example.

questions.question: Write the sample space when two coins are tossed together, and state n(S).
questions.answer:
Each coin can show a head (H) or a tail (T). Listing all combinations of the first and second coin:
   S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
There are four sample points, so n(S) = 4.
questions.explanation: List the four ordered outcomes; n(S)=4.

questions.question: A die is thrown. Write the sample space and list the outcomes of the event A = 'a number greater than 4 appears'. Is A simple or compound?
questions.answer:
Sample space: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, so n(S) = 6.
The event A = 'a number greater than 4' = {5, 6}.
Since A contains more than one outcome (two sample points), A is a COMPOUND event.
questions.explanation: S has 6 points; A = {5,6}; more than one outcome => compound.

questions.question: In the throw of a die, let A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {1, 2, 3}. Find A union B, A intersect B and A'.
questions.answer:
A = {2, 4, 6} (even numbers), B = {1, 2, 3}.
A union B = all outcomes in A or B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}.
A intersect B = outcomes common to both = {2}.
A' = outcomes of S not in A = {1, 3, 5}.
questions.explanation: Union = combine; intersection = common; complement = rest of S.

questions.question: Explain, with an example from the throw of a die, what is meant by mutually exclusive events.
questions.answer:
Two events are mutually exclusive (disjoint) if they cannot occur together, i.e. they have no outcome in common, so A intersect B = empty set.
Example: in the throw of a die let A = 'an even number' = {2, 4, 6} and C = 'an odd number' = {1, 3, 5}. No number is both even and odd, so A intersect C = empty set. Hence A and C are mutually exclusive - on any single throw at most one of them can occur.
questions.explanation: No common outcome; even and odd on a die.

questions.question: Give an example of a sure event and an impossible event in the throw of a single die, and explain why each is so.
questions.answer:
Sure (certain) event: 'getting a number less than 7' = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S. It contains every outcome, so it must occur on every throw - hence it is certain.
Impossible event: 'getting a 7'. No face of a die shows 7, so the corresponding subset has no outcomes (it is the empty set) and can never occur.
questions.explanation: Sure = whole S; impossible = empty set.

questions.question: Two dice are thrown. Write the event 'the sum of the numbers is 7' and state how many outcomes it contains.
questions.answer:
Each outcome is an ordered pair (first die, second die). The pairs whose sum is 7 are:
   {(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)}.
This event contains 6 outcomes. (The total sample space has n(S) = 36 outcomes.)
questions.explanation: List ordered pairs summing to 7; 6 outcomes.

questions.question: For the throw of a die, let A = {1, 2}, B = {3, 4} and C = {5, 6}. Show that A, B, C form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system. Explain both properties.
questions.answer:
Sample space: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
Mutually exclusive: taking the events in pairs,
   A intersect B = empty, B intersect C = empty, A intersect C = empty.
No two of the events share a common outcome, so they are mutually exclusive (pairwise disjoint) - at most one of them can occur on a single throw.
Exhaustive: their union is
   A union B union C = {1, 2} union {3, 4} union {5, 6} = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S.
Together they include every possible outcome, so they are exhaustive - at least one of them must occur.
Since the three events are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive, they form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system (a partition) of S: every outcome of S belongs to exactly one of A, B, C.
questions.explanation: Pairwise intersections empty (exclusive) and union = S (exhaustive) => partition.

questions.question: What is meant by equally likely outcomes? Give one example and one non-example.
questions.answer:
Outcomes are equally likely if there is no reason to expect any one in preference to another - each has the same chance of occurring.
Example: for a fair (unbiased) coin, head and tail are equally likely; for a fair die the six faces are equally likely.
Non-example: for a biased (loaded) die that is weighted to favour the six, the outcomes are NOT equally likely, because one face has a greater chance than the others.
questions.explanation: Same chance; fair coin/die vs biased die.

questions.question: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. Let A = 'the card is a king' and B = 'the card is a spade'. Describe the sample space size, find n(A), n(B) and n(A intersect B), and describe in words the events A union B and A intersect B.
questions.answer:
Sample space: a pack has 52 cards, so n(S) = 52, and each card is equally likely.
n(A): there are 4 kings, so n(A) = 4.
n(B): there are 13 spades, so n(B) = 13.
A intersect B: the card that is both a king and a spade is the single king of spades, so n(A intersect B) = 1.
A union B in words: 'the card is a king OR a spade (or both)'. Its outcomes are the 4 kings together with the 13 spades, with the king of spades counted once; the number of outcomes is n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B) = 4 + 13 - 1 = 16.
A intersect B in words: 'the card is a king AND a spade', i.e. exactly the king of spades - a single outcome.
questions.explanation: n(S)=52; kings 4, spades 13, overlap 1; union 16 cards; intersection = king of spades.

questions.question: Distinguish between a deterministic experiment and a random experiment.
questions.answer: A deterministic experiment is one whose result is certain and can be predicted exactly under given conditions - for example, heating water to 100 C at normal pressure always makes it boil. A random experiment can be repeated under identical conditions and has all its outcomes known in advance, but the particular result of any trial cannot be predicted - for example, tossing a coin.
questions.explanation: Deterministic = predictable; random = unpredictable result.

questions.question: Define the terms 'trial' and 'outcome' with an example.
questions.answer: A trial is a single performance of a random experiment; an outcome is the result of that trial. For example, throwing a die once is a trial, and getting a 4 is an outcome. Each outcome is one of the possible elementary results and is also called a sample point.
questions.explanation: Trial = one performance; outcome = its result.

questions.question: State whether the following is a random experiment and why: 'observing the number shown when a fair die is rolled'.
questions.answer: Yes, it is a random experiment. It can be repeated under identical conditions, all its outcomes {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} are known in advance, but the particular number shown on any roll cannot be predicted with certainty. These three properties make it a random experiment.
questions.explanation: Repeatable + outcomes known + unpredictable => random.

questions.question: Write the sample space for tossing three coins and state n(S).
questions.answer:
Each coin shows H or T. Listing all combinations:
   S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT}.
There are 8 outcomes, so n(S) = 8 (= 2^3).
questions.explanation: 2^3 = 8 outcomes listed.

questions.question: What is meant by a finite and an infinite sample space? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: A finite sample space has a limited, countable number of outcomes - for example, throwing a die gives S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, a finite set. An infinite sample space has unlimited outcomes - for example, tossing a coin repeatedly until the first head appears, where the number of tosses could be 1, 2, 3, ... without any largest value.
questions.explanation: Finite = limited (die); infinite = unlimited (tosses until first head).

questions.question: A coin and a die are tossed together. Write the sample space and state n(S).
questions.answer:
Each outcome is a pair (coin result, die result). With the coin showing H or T and the die 1 to 6:
   S = {(H,1),(H,2),(H,3),(H,4),(H,5),(H,6),(T,1),(T,2),(T,3),(T,4),(T,5),(T,6)}.
There are 2 x 6 = 12 outcomes, so n(S) = 12.
questions.explanation: 2 x 6 = 12 ordered pairs.

questions.question: Two dice are thrown. List the outcomes of the event 'the sum of the numbers is 5' and state how many there are.
questions.answer:
Writing each outcome as (first die, second die), the pairs summing to 5 are:
   {(1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1)}.
There are 4 such outcomes.
questions.explanation: Four ordered pairs sum to 5.

questions.question: Two coins are tossed. Write the event 'at least one tail' and state the number of favourable outcomes.
questions.answer:
S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. 'At least one tail' means one or two tails:
   {HT, TH, TT}.
The number of favourable outcomes is 3.
questions.explanation: All outcomes except HH; 3 outcomes.

questions.question: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Write, in words and as counts, the events 'a red card', 'a face card' and 'a red face card'.
questions.answer:
'A red card' = hearts and diamonds = 26 cards, so n = 26.
'A face card' = jacks, queens and kings of all four suits = 12 cards, so n = 12.
'A red face card' = the face cards of hearts and diamonds = 6 cards (J, Q, K of hearts and of diamonds), so n = 6.
questions.explanation: Red 26, face 12, red face 6.

questions.question: A bag contains 4 white and 3 black balls, all distinct. Write n(S) for drawing one ball, and n(A) for the event 'a white ball'.
questions.answer: There are 4 + 3 = 7 distinct balls, so drawing one ball gives n(S) = 7. The event A = 'a white ball' has 4 favourable outcomes, so n(A) = 4.

questions.question: Define a simple event and a compound event with an example each from the throw of a die.
questions.answer: A simple (elementary) event contains exactly one outcome - for example, 'getting a 3' = {3}. A compound event contains more than one outcome - for example, 'getting an even number' = {2, 4, 6}, which is made up of several sample points.
questions.explanation: Simple = one outcome; compound = several.

questions.question: Explain, with examples from a die, the difference between a sure event and an impossible event.
questions.answer: A sure (certain) event is certain to occur because it contains every outcome; it equals S. Example: 'getting a number from 1 to 6' = {1,2,3,4,5,6} = S. An impossible event can never occur because it contains no outcome; it is the empty set. Example: 'getting a 7' on a die.
questions.explanation: Sure = S; impossible = empty set.

questions.question: For the event A = 'a multiple of 3' in the throw of a die, write A, A', and verify n(A) + n(A') = n(S).
questions.answer:
S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, n(S) = 6.
A = 'a multiple of 3' = {3, 6}, so n(A) = 2.
A' = 'not a multiple of 3' = {1, 2, 4, 5}, so n(A') = 4.
Then n(A) + n(A') = 2 + 4 = 6 = n(S). Verified.

questions.question: What is a complementary event? State the relation between an event and its complement.
questions.answer: The complement of an event A, written A' (or 'not A'), is the set of all outcomes of the sample space that are not in A. It occurs exactly when A does not occur. An event and its complement satisfy A union A' = S and A intersect A' = empty set, and n(A) + n(A') = n(S).
questions.explanation: A' = not A; A U A' = S, A n A' = empty.

questions.question: In the throw of a die, A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. Find A union B, A intersect B and A - B.
questions.answer:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, B = {3, 4, 5}.
A union B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} (all outcomes in A or B).
A intersect B = {3, 4} (common outcomes).
A - B = {1, 2} (in A but not in B).
questions.explanation: Union, intersection and difference computed.

questions.question: Express the following events in set notation using A and B: (i) 'A but not B', (ii) 'neither A nor B'.
questions.answer:
(i) 'A but not B' = A intersect B' (equivalently A - B).
(ii) 'neither A nor B' = A' intersect B' = (A union B)' by De Morgan's law.
questions.explanation: A but not B = A n B'; neither = (A U B)'.

questions.question: State De Morgan's laws for two events A and B, and illustrate the first with A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3} in the throw of a die.
questions.answer:
De Morgan's laws: (A union B)' = A' intersect B' and (A intersect B)' = A' union B'.
Illustration: S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. A union B = {1, 2, 3}, so (A union B)' = {4, 5, 6}. Also A' = {3, 4, 5, 6} and B' = {1, 4, 5, 6}, so A' intersect B' = {4, 5, 6}. Both sides equal {4, 5, 6}, verifying the first law.
questions.explanation: Both laws stated; first verified giving {4,5,6}.

questions.question: Define exhaustive events and give one example from the throw of a die.
questions.answer: A set of events is exhaustive if together they include every possible outcome, i.e. their union is the whole sample space S. Example: in the throw of a die, A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5, 6} are exhaustive because A union B = {1,2,3,4,5,6} = S, so at least one of them must occur.
questions.explanation: Union = S; example A={1,2,3}, B={4,5,6}.

questions.question: Why are an event A and its complement A' always both mutually exclusive and exhaustive?
questions.answer: They are mutually exclusive because no outcome can be both in A and not in A, so A intersect A' = empty set. They are exhaustive because every outcome is either in A or not in A, so A union A' = S. Hence A and A' always form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system (partition) of S.
questions.explanation: A n A' = empty and A U A' = S.

questions.question: In the throw of a die, decide whether A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6} are (i) mutually exclusive, (ii) exhaustive. Justify.
questions.answer:
(i) A intersect B = {3}, which is not empty, so A and B are NOT mutually exclusive (they can occur together when the outcome is 3).
(ii) A union B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S, so A and B ARE exhaustive - at least one of them always occurs.
Thus the events are exhaustive but not mutually exclusive.
questions.explanation: Overlap {3} => not exclusive; union = S => exhaustive.

questions.question: Determine whether the events A = {1, 2}, B = {3, 4} and C = {5, 6} form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system for a die, and state what such a system is called.
questions.answer:
Mutually exclusive: A intersect B = empty, B intersect C = empty and A intersect C = empty, so the events are pairwise disjoint.
Exhaustive: A union B union C = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S.
Since the events are both pairwise mutually exclusive and exhaustive, they form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system, also called a PARTITION of the sample space; every outcome belongs to exactly one of A, B, C.
questions.explanation: Pairwise disjoint + union S => partition.

questions.question: What are equally likely outcomes? State the condition on a coin or die for its outcomes to be equally likely.
questions.answer: Outcomes are equally likely if there is no reason to expect any one in preference to another, so each has the same chance of occurring. A coin's outcomes (head, tail) are equally likely when the coin is unbiased (fair); a die's six outcomes are equally likely when the die is fair (not loaded). If the coin or die is biased, the outcomes are not equally likely.
questions.explanation: Same chance; requires a fair/unbiased coin or die.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by a random experiment. State its defining conditions, distinguish it from a deterministic experiment, and give two examples of each.
questions.answer:
A random (or probabilistic) experiment is an experiment whose particular result cannot be predicted with certainty even though the complete list of possible results is known. It is defined by three conditions:
(i) it can be repeated any number of times under identical conditions;
(ii) all its possible outcomes are known in advance; and
(iii) the actual outcome on any particular trial cannot be predicted with certainty.
A deterministic experiment, in contrast, always produces the same result under fixed conditions, so its outcome can be predicted exactly.
Examples of random experiments: (1) tossing a coin - the outcomes are head and tail but which appears cannot be foretold; (2) throwing a die - the outcomes are 1 to 6 but the face shown is unpredictable.
Examples of deterministic experiments: (1) heating water to 100 C at normal atmospheric pressure always makes it boil; (2) combining hydrogen and oxygen under fixed conditions always gives water. The key difference is predictability: a deterministic result is certain, a random result is not.
questions.explanation: Three conditions; random vs deterministic; two examples each.

questions.question: Describe how to write the sample space of a random experiment. Write the sample spaces for (a) tossing two coins, (b) throwing two dice, and state n(S) in each case.
questions.answer:
The sample space S of a random experiment is the set of ALL possible outcomes; each element is a sample point and n(S) is the number of sample points. To write it, list every distinct result that the experiment can produce, using ordered symbols where the order matters.
(a) Tossing two coins: each coin shows H or T, so
   S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, and n(S) = 4.
(b) Throwing two dice: each outcome is an ordered pair (first die, second die) with each entry from 1 to 6, so
   S = {(1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (1,5), (1,6), (2,1), ..., (6,6)}.
There are 6 choices for the first die and 6 for the second, giving n(S) = 6 x 6 = 36.
In each case, once S is written, any event can be described simply as a subset of S.
questions.explanation: Method + two coins (4) + two dice (36).

questions.question: Explain the different types of events with examples from the throw of a single die: simple, compound, sure, impossible and complementary.
questions.answer:
In the throw of a die, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
Simple (elementary) event: contains exactly one outcome, e.g. 'getting a 4' = {4}.
Compound event: contains more than one outcome, e.g. 'getting an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
Sure (certain) event: certain to occur, containing all outcomes, e.g. 'getting a number less than 7' = {1,2,3,4,5,6} = S.
Impossible event: can never occur, containing no outcome, e.g. 'getting a 7' = empty set.
Complementary event: for an event A, its complement A' is 'not A', the outcomes of S not in A. For A = {2, 4, 6}, A' = {1, 3, 5}. An event and its complement satisfy A union A' = S and A intersect A' = empty set, with n(A) + n(A') = n(S). These types together let us classify any subset of the sample space.
questions.explanation: All five types defined with die examples.

questions.question: In the throw of a die let A = 'an even number' and B = 'a number greater than 3'. Write A and B, then find A union B, A intersect B, A', B - A, and describe each in words.
questions.answer:
S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
A = 'an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
B = 'a number greater than 3' = {4, 5, 6}.
A union B = {2, 4, 5, 6}: the outcome is even OR greater than 3 (at least one holds).
A intersect B = {4, 6}: the outcome is even AND greater than 3 (both hold).
A' = {1, 3, 5}: the outcome is NOT even (an odd number).
B - A = B intersect A' = {5}: the outcome is greater than 3 but NOT even (i.e. 5).
Thus every verbal statement about the die - 'or', 'and', 'not', 'but not' - corresponds to a set operation on the events, which is the whole point of the algebra of events.
questions.explanation: A={2,4,6}, B={4,5,6}; union, intersection, complement, difference with descriptions.

questions.question: State the main identities and laws of the algebra of events for two events A and B of a sample space S, and give the meaning of A intersect B' in words.
questions.answer:
For events A and B of a sample space S the following hold:
- A union A' = S and A intersect A' = empty set.
- (A')' = A.
- Commutative: A union B = B union A and A intersect B = B intersect A.
- De Morgan's laws: (A union B)' = A' intersect B' and (A intersect B)' = A' union B'.
- Difference: A - B = A intersect B'.
Meaning of A intersect B': it is the event that A occurs but B does NOT occur - the outcomes that belong to A and at the same time do not belong to B. For example, if A = {1,2,3} and B = {2,3,4} then A intersect B' = {1}, i.e. the outcome is in A but not in B.
questions.explanation: Key identities + De Morgan + A n B' = 'A but not B'.

questions.question: Define mutually exclusive events and exhaustive events. Using the throw of a die, give an example that is mutually exclusive but not exhaustive, one that is exhaustive but not mutually exclusive, and one that is both.
questions.answer:
Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events cannot occur together: their intersection is the empty set. Exhaustive events together cover the whole sample space: their union is S.
For a die, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
Mutually exclusive but not exhaustive: A = {1, 2} and B = {3, 4}. Here A intersect B = empty (exclusive), but A union B = {1, 2, 3, 4} is not S (5 and 6 are missing), so not exhaustive.
Exhaustive but not mutually exclusive: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}. Here A union B = S (exhaustive), but A intersect B = {3, 4} is not empty, so not mutually exclusive.
Both mutually exclusive and exhaustive: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5, 6}. Here A intersect B = empty and A union B = S, so they partition the sample space.
questions.explanation: Definitions + one example of each combination.

questions.question: Explain what a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system (partition) of a sample space is. Verify that the events A = {2, 4, 6}, B = {1, 3} and C = {5} form such a system for the throw of a die, and explain what it means for each outcome.
questions.answer:
A mutually exclusive and exhaustive system (a partition) of a sample space S is a collection of events that are pairwise mutually exclusive (no two share an outcome) AND together exhaustive (their union is S). Consequently every outcome of S belongs to EXACTLY ONE of the events.
Verification for S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} with A = {2, 4, 6}, B = {1, 3}, C = {5}:
Mutually exclusive: A intersect B = empty, B intersect C = empty, A intersect C = empty (no common outcomes in any pair).
Exhaustive: A union B union C = {2, 4, 6} union {1, 3} union {5} = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S.
Since both properties hold, A, B, C form a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system.
Meaning for each outcome: every number on the die falls into exactly one of the three events - for example 4 is in A only, 3 is in B only, 5 is in C only - so the three events cleanly split the sample space with no gaps and no overlaps.
questions.explanation: Definition of partition + verify disjoint and union = S; each outcome in exactly one event.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of equally likely outcomes and their role in the classical description of probability. Discuss with examples of fair and biased experiments.
questions.answer:
Outcomes are equally likely if, by the symmetry of the experiment, there is no reason to expect any one in preference to another, so each has the same chance of occurring. This is a modelling assumption about the physical symmetry of the experiment, not something proved by logic.
Examples of fair (unbiased) experiments where outcomes are equally likely: a fair coin (head and tail equally likely), a fair die (the six faces equally likely), and a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards (each card equally likely to be drawn).
Examples of biased experiments where outcomes are NOT equally likely: a loaded die weighted to favour one face, or a bent coin that lands on one side more often.
Role in probability: the classical (or 'a priori') definition of probability applies only when outcomes are equally likely. It defines the probability of an event A as
   P(A) = (number of outcomes favourable to A) / (total number of equally likely outcomes) = n(A) / n(S).
Thus the equally likely assumption provides the symmetry that makes this simple counting definition valid; when it fails, probabilities must be found by other methods.
questions.explanation: Equally likely = same chance; fair vs biased; P(A) = n(A)/n(S).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
An experiment is called random if it can be repeated under identical conditions, all its outcomes are known in advance, but the particular result cannot be predicted. A trial is one performance and its result is an outcome. Consider the experiment of throwing an ordinary die once.
(a) Is this a random experiment? Give one reason.
(b) What is a trial in this experiment?
(c) Name any two possible outcomes.
(d) Give one example of a deterministic experiment for contrast.
questions.answer:
(a) Yes. It is repeatable under identical conditions, its outcomes {1,2,3,4,5,6} are known, but the particular face shown cannot be predicted - so it is random.
(b) A trial is one throw of the die.
(c) Any two of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 - for example, getting a 2 and getting a 5.
(d) A deterministic experiment: heating water to 100 C at normal pressure, which always makes it boil (a certain, predictable result).
questions.explanation: Random (unpredictable result); trial = one throw; outcomes 1-6; deterministic contrast.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The sample space S of a random experiment is the set of all possible outcomes, and n(S) is the number of sample points. When n coins are tossed there are 2^n outcomes.
(a) Write the sample space for tossing two coins.
(b) State n(S) for tossing three coins.
(c) How many outcomes are there for tossing four coins?
(d) What is meant by a sample point?
questions.answer:
(a) S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
(b) For three coins, n(S) = 2^3 = 8.
(c) For four coins, the number of outcomes is 2^4 = 16.
(d) A sample point is a single outcome (element) of the sample space.
questions.explanation: Two coins listed; 2^3 = 8; 2^4 = 16; sample point = one outcome.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two dice are thrown together and each outcome is written as an ordered pair (first die, second die). The sample space has 36 outcomes.
(a) How many outcomes have both dice showing the same number?
(b) List the outcomes whose sum is 9.
(c) How many outcomes have a sum of 7?
(d) Write the event 'the first die shows 6' and state how many outcomes it has.
questions.explanation: Doubles 6; sum 9 has 4; sum 7 has 6; first die 6 has 6.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
An event is a subset of the sample space. Events may be simple (one outcome), compound (more than one), sure (equal to S), impossible (the empty set) or complementary (A'). Consider the throw of a die with S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}.
(a) Classify the event {4} and the event {2,4,6}.
(b) Give an example of a sure event and an impossible event.
(c) If A = {1,2}, write A'.
(d) Verify n(A) + n(A') = n(S) for this A.
questions.answer:
(a) {4} is a simple (elementary) event; {2, 4, 6} is a compound event.
(b) Sure event: 'a number from 1 to 6' = S; impossible event: 'getting a 7' = empty set.
(c) A' = {3, 4, 5, 6}.
(d) n(A) = 2 and n(A') = 4, so n(A) + n(A') = 2 + 4 = 6 = n(S). Verified.
questions.explanation: Simple vs compound; sure = S, impossible = empty; A' = {3,4,5,6}; 2+4=6.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Events can be combined by set operations: union A U B ('A or B'), intersection A n B ('A and B'), complement A' ('not A') and difference A - B = A intersect B' ('A but not B'). In the throw of a die let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 4, 6}.
(a) Find A union B.
(b) Find A intersect B.
(c) Find A - B.
(d) Write A' and describe it in words.
questions.answer:
(a) A union B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}.
(b) A intersect B = {2}.
(c) A - B = A intersect B' = {1, 3}.
(d) A' = {4, 5, 6}, i.e. the outcomes that are NOT in A = {1, 2, 3} - the numbers greater than 3.
questions.explanation: Union {1,2,3,4,6}; intersection {2}; difference {1,3}; complement {4,5,6}.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
De Morgan's laws state that (A union B)' = A' intersect B' and (A intersect B)' = A' union B'. In the throw of a die take A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}.
(a) Find A union B and then (A union B)'.
(b) Find A' and B'.
(c) Verify the first De Morgan law.
(d) Express 'neither A nor B' in set notation.
questions.answer:
(a) A union B = {1, 2, 3, 4}, so (A union B)' = {5, 6}.
(b) A' = {4, 5, 6} and B' = {1, 2, 5, 6}.
(c) A' intersect B' = {5, 6}, which equals (A union B)' = {5, 6}. So the first law holds.
(d) 'Neither A nor B' = A' intersect B' = (A union B)' = {5, 6}.
questions.explanation: (A U B)' = {5,6} = A' n B'; neither = (A U B)'.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur together (A intersect B = empty). A set of events is exhaustive if their union is S. In the throw of a die consider A = {1, 3, 5} (odd) and B = {2, 4, 6} (even).
(a) Are A and B mutually exclusive? Justify.
(b) Are A and B exhaustive? Justify.
(c) What is B in relation to A?
(d) State the value of n(A) + n(B).
questions.answer:
(a) Yes. A intersect B = empty set (no number is both odd and even), so they are mutually exclusive.
(b) Yes. A union B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S, so they are exhaustive.
(c) B is the complement of A, i.e. B = A' (the even numbers are exactly the 'not odd' outcomes).
(d) n(A) + n(B) = 3 + 3 = 6 = n(S).
questions.explanation: Odd and even: disjoint, union S, B = A', total 6.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A collection of events is a mutually exclusive and exhaustive system (partition) if the events are pairwise disjoint and their union is S. In the throw of a die consider the collection A = {1, 2}, B = {2, 3, 4}, C = {5, 6}.
(a) Is this collection mutually exclusive? Justify.
(b) Is it exhaustive? Justify.
(c) Does it form a partition of S?
(d) Modify B so that the three events form a valid partition.
questions.answer:
(a) No. A intersect B = {2} is not empty, so the events are not pairwise disjoint - they are not mutually exclusive.
(b) Yes. A union B union C = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S, so the collection is exhaustive.
(c) No. Because it fails to be mutually exclusive, it is not a partition (the outcome 2 lies in two events).
(d) Change B to {3, 4}. Then A = {1, 2}, B = {3, 4}, C = {5, 6} are pairwise disjoint and their union is S, so they form a valid partition.
questions.explanation: Overlap at 2 => not exclusive; union S; fix B = {3,4} to partition.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Outcomes are equally likely if each has the same chance of occurring, as for a fair coin, a fair die, or a well-shuffled pack. The classical probability of an event A is P(A) = n(A)/n(S) when outcomes are equally likely.
(a) Are the outcomes of a fair die equally likely?
(b) Are the outcomes of a loaded die equally likely?
(c) For a fair die, use the classical formula to find the probability of an even number.
(d) State the assumption that the classical formula requires.
questions.answer:
(a) Yes. For a fair die the six faces have the same chance, so the outcomes are equally likely.
(b) No. A loaded die favours some faces, so its outcomes are not equally likely.
(c) Even numbers = {2, 4, 6}, so n(A) = 3 and n(S) = 6, giving P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2.
(d) It requires that all the outcomes of the sample space be equally likely.
questions.explanation: Fair die equally likely; loaded not; P(even) = 1/2; needs equally likely outcomes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. The pack has four suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs), each of 13 cards, and the 52 cards are equally likely to be drawn.
(a) State n(S).
(b) Write n(A) for A = 'the card is a heart'.
(c) Write n(B) for B = 'the card is an ace'.
(d) How many cards are both a heart and an ace, i.e. n(A intersect B)?
questions.answer:
(a) n(S) = 52 (the whole pack).
(b) There are 13 hearts, so n(A) = 13.
(c) There are 4 aces (one per suit), so n(B) = 4.
(d) Only the ace of hearts is both a heart and an ace, so n(A intersect B) = 1.
questions.explanation: n(S)=52; hearts 13; aces 4; heart-and-ace = 1.
